                                          ORDER ON COMPLAINT

                                           (Issued March 19, 2026)

                On December 29, 2025, Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC
         (NIPSCO) filed a complaint (Complaint) pursuant to sections 202(c), 306, and 309 of the
         Federal Power Act (FPA)1 and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and
         Procedure,2 proposing revisions to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.
         (MISO) Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff
         (Tariff) to add a provision (Proposed Tariff Provision) to allocate the costs of keeping
         Units 17 and 18 of the Schahfer generating plant (collectively, Schahfer Units) in
         operation, in response to the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) December 23, 2025
         Emergency Order No. 202-25-12 (DOE Order), under section 202(c) of the FPA and
         section 301 of the DOE Organization Act.3

                 In this order, we grant the Complaint and find that the Proposed Tariff
         Provision is just and reasonable, subject to modification and to the outcome of the
         proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425. We direct MISO to make a compliance filing,
         within 30 days of the date of a Commission order accepting MISO’s compliance
         filing in Docket No. ER25-3425, to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision, as revised, as
         discussed below.

         I.     Background

                A.        Schahfer Units Retirement Plan

                The Schahfer Units, located in northwestern Indiana, are coal-fired units that each
         have a maximum capacity of 437.5 MW. NIPSCO planned to retire the units on
         December 31, 2025, pursuant to settlement agreements approved by the Indiana Utility
         Regulatory Commission (Indiana Commission) in 2023 and 2025.4 NIPSCO submitted a
         notice to suspend operation of the Schahfer Units to MISO pursuant to Attachment Y of
         the Tariff, and MISO found no reliability violations.

                B.        DOE Order

                In the DOE Order, the Secretary of Energy determined that “an emergency exists
         in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric
         energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electric energy, and other causes.”5
         Further, the Secretary of Energy determined that issuance of the DOE Order will “meet
         the emergency and serve the public interest.”6 Therefore, the Secretary of Energy
         directed MISO and NIPSCO to take all measures necessary to ensure that the Schahfer
         Units were available to operate7 and directed NIPSCO to keep the Schahfer Units open
         for 90 days, i.e., until March 23, 2026.8

                 The DOE Order cited a statement in the 2024 North American Electric Reliability
         Corporation (NERC) Long-Term Reliability Assessment (Reliability Assessment) that
         MISO is at risk because “probabilistic assessments indicate above-normal generator
         outages during extreme weather can result in unserved energy or load loss. With
         uncertainty around new resource additions and existing generator retirements, MISO is
         also at risk of falling below [Reference Margin Levels] within the next five years.”9 The
         DOE Order quoted a MISO April 2025 presentation on the Planning Resource Auction

         Tariff provision approved by the Commission with regard to the Consumers Energy
         Company (Consumers) J.H. Campbell plant (Campbell Plant), and the geographic scope

         emergency order on the Campbell Plant (Campbell Plant DOE Order).17

               B.        Comments and Protests

                 The Michigan Attorney General and the Illinois Commission state that, contrary to
         claims made by the DOE Order, there is no evidence of an energy emergency.26 The
         Illinois Commission asserts that MISO does not need the capacity provided by the
         Schahfer Units and that MISO has emergency operating procedures, which both belie the
         notion of an emergency in MISO.27 The Illinois Commission further states that the DOE
         Order is an overreach of federal authority because it encroaches on that state’s role in
         resource adequacy and fuel choice.28

         that the Commission should reject it because the underlying DOE Order justifying cost
         recovery is ultra vires, and, absent a valid legal obligation to operate pursuant to FPA

         pursuant to FPA sections 205 or 206 is not just and reasonable and is unduly
         discriminatory or preferential, and violates the filed rate doctrine. Alternatively, the
         Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission, under the discretion afforded
         the Commission under FPA section 202(c), issue an order deferring any finding, on the
         basis that the Proposed Tariff Provision is premature until the rehearing requests at DOE
         are resolved.29 The Michigan Attorney General also asserts that the Commission should
         limit cost recovery to those costs from the limited scope of operation ordered by the DOE
         Order if the Commission accepts the Proposed Tariff Provision.30 The Michigan
         Attorney General notes that the DOE Order requires that MISO “take every step to
         employ economic dispatch” of the Schahfer Units in order “to minimize cost to
         ratepayers” and argues that any form of commitment and dispatch that enables the

                 The Commission’s rate analysis applies the cost causation principle, which
         requires that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the
         customer who must pay them.”66 We find that this is the relevant legal standard for
         evaluating whether the proposed method to allocate the costs of keeping the Schahfer
         Units in operation, in response to the DOE Order, is just and reasonable. Courts have
         explained that, to “the extent that a utility benefits from the costs of new facilities, it may
         be said to have ‘caused’ a part of those costs to be incurred, as without the expectation of
         its contributions the facilities might not have been built, or might have been delayed.”67
         As a result, a cost allocation method can satisfy the cost causation principle if the
         Commission “has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are at
         least roughly commensurate with” the allocation of the costs.68
